stem: A 34-year-old with gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 4 months. She reports galactorrhea and missed periods. Pregnancy test is negative and prolactin is elevated. What is the most likely cause?
correct: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine, the brake on prolactin

distractors.text: A prolactinoma that now needs cabergoline twice weekly
distractors.why: A drug cause must be excluded first; she takes a dopamine blocker.

distractors.text: Metoclopramide stimulates dopamine, raising prolactin release
distractors.why: Dopamine inhibits prolactin; the drug blocks it.

distractors.text: Estrogen excess raising thyroid-binding globulin levels
distractors.why: That changes levothyroxine needs, not prolactin.

distractors.text: Primary hypothyroidism from an undetected drug interaction
distractors.why: Nothing here points to thyroid drugs or disease.

why_correct: Dopamine is the brake on prolactin. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide block dopamine, so prolactin rises.
takeaway: Dopamine blockers raise prolactin.
discriminator: Cabergoline restores the brake; metoclopramide removes it.

stem: A 41-year-old with untreated Graves disease arrives with fever 40°C, heart rate 158, agitation and vomiting after an infection. Propranolol has been given. Which sequence is correct for the next drugs?

distractors.text: Iodine now, PTU 1 hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
distractors.why: Iodine before PTU supplies substrate for new hormone.

distractors.text: PTU now, aspirin for the fever, then iodine an hour later
distractors.why: Aspirin frees bound hormone and is avoided in storm.

distractors.text: Methimazole now, with levothyroxine held until afterwards
distractors.why: The storm sequence taught is PTU first, then iodine.

distractors.text: Hydrocortisone alone, since it blocks all hormone release
distractors.why: Steroids help conversion and adrenal cover; they are added.

why_correct: Beta-blocker and PTU come first; iodine is given only after PTU because iodine first would feed new hormone synthesis. Steroids blunt peripheral conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency. Aspirin is avoided.
takeaway: Storm order: beta-blocker + PTU, then iodine, plus steroid.
discriminator: PTU blocks synthesis; iodine blocks release, but only after PTU.

stem: An 81-year-old on metformin has A1c above goal. She lives alone and has fallen twice this year. Which add-on fits the lecture's reasoning?
correct: Sitagliptin, because its hypoglycemia risk is low

distractors.text: Glipizide, because it is the most potent oral option
distractors.why: Sulfonylureas carry the highest oral hypoglycemia risk.

distractors.text: Repaglinide, because mealtime dosing prevents all lows
distractors.why: It is still a secretagogue.

distractors.text: Pioglitazone, because fluid retention protects from falls
distractors.why: Fluid retention and heart failure are its risks.

distractors.text: Semaglutide plus sitagliptin, to cover both incretin steps
distractors.why: A GLP-1 RA is not combined with a DPP-4 inhibitor.

why_correct: For an older adult who falls, choose the safest drug, not the most potent. Sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release; a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable.
takeaway: Falls + diabetes: avoid sulfonylureas.
discriminator: Glucose-dependent drugs rarely cause lows; secretagogues do.

stem: A 39-year-old with Cushing syndrome and type 2 diabetes starts mifepristone. A month later her glucose control is better, but serum cortisol is higher than before. Which interpretation is correct?

distractors.why: Pancreatitis and gallstones are GLP-1 RA concerns.

takeaway: Sick on an SGLT2 inhibitor: think DKA even with normal glucose.

stem: A 58-year-old has taken prednisone daily for 8 months for polymyalgia. He ran out 4 days ago. He presents with vomiting, weakness and blood pressure 82/50. What explains this, and what is the treatment?

stem: A 71-year-old started desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus 10 days ago. To 'stay hydrated' he drinks water all day. He is now confused with a headache and nausea. Which step is most appropriate first?
correct: Check serum sodium for desmopressin hyponatremia

distractors.text: Add tolvaptan to speed water excretion at home
distractors.why: Tolvaptan is for SIADH and is started in hospital.

distractors.text: Raise the desmopressin dose for incomplete control
distractors.why: More drug would retain more water.

distractors.text: Check liver tests for desmopressin hepatotoxicity
distractors.why: Liver injury is the tolvaptan concern.

distractors.text: Start demeclocycline to counter the retained water
distractors.why: Demeclocycline is a refractory-SIADH option.

why_correct: Desmopressin keeps free water in. The risk is hyponatremia, so sodium is monitored and fluids are limited.
takeaway: Desmopressin: monitor sodium, limit fluids.
discriminator: Desmopressin → hyponatremia; tolvaptan → overcorrection and liver injury.

stem: A patient with acromegaly switches from octreotide to pegvisomant. Three months later IGF-1 is normal, but MRI shows the adenoma unchanged in size. Which statement explains both findings?
correct: It blocks the GH receptor: IGF-1 falls, tumor untouched

distractors.text: It lowers GH release, so the tumor should shrink with time
distractors.why: That describes octreotide and lanreotide.

distractors.text: It restores dopamine tone, so prolactin and GH both fall
distractors.why: That describes cabergoline in prolactinoma.

distractors.text: It blocks IGF-1 itself, so GH and the tumor are suppressed
distractors.why: Its target is the GH receptor, not IGF-1.

distractors.text: It replaces GH, so feedback switches the adenoma off
distractors.why: Somatropin replaces GH and is for deficiency.

why_correct: Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so the liver makes less IGF-1. It does not act on the pituitary, so it does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.
takeaway: Pegvisomant fixes the lab, not the tumor.
discriminator: Octreotide lowers GH release; pegvisomant blocks its receptor.

stem: A 48-year-old on a stable levothyroxine dose has TSH 9.8 mIU/L. She takes it every morning with breakfast, her calcium carbonate and a new iron tablet. She has not missed a dose. What is the best next step?
correct: Take it on an empty stomach, 4 h from calcium and iron

distractors.text: Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 2 weeks
distractors.why: Fix absorption first; TSH is rechecked at 6–8 weeks.

distractors.text: Switch to methimazole because the levothyroxine has failed
distractors.why: Methimazole treats hyperthyroidism.

distractors.text: Move the dose to dinner so it is taken with the largest meal
distractors.why: Food reduces absorption; it is taken on an empty stomach.

distractors.text: Stop the iron permanently because the two can never be combined
distractors.why: They can be combined when separated by 4 hours.

why_correct: Calcium, iron and antacids reduce levothyroxine absorption. Take it 30–60 minutes before breakfast and separate those products by at least 4 hours, then check TSH at 6–8 weeks.
takeaway: High TSH on levothyroxine: check timing before raising the dose.
discriminator: Absorption problem (binders) vs clearance problem (inducers).

stem: A 52-year-old with acromegaly has taken octreotide for a year. IGF-1 is at goal. He now reports episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals and a resting pulse of 52. Which explanation fits best?
correct: Expected octreotide effects: gallstones and bradycardia

distractors.text: Pegvisomant toxicity: liver injury needing liver tests
distractors.why: He takes octreotide; liver tests are the pegvisomant concern.

distractors.text: Cabergoline effect: orthostatic hypotension and nausea
distractors.why: Those are dopamine-agonist effects, not his drug.

distractors.text: Tumor growth: the pituitary mass is pressing locally
distractors.why: IGF-1 is at goal and the symptoms are biliary.

distractors.text: Desmopressin effect: hyponatremia from retained water
distractors.why: He is not on desmopressin and has no sodium symptoms.

why_correct: Octreotide and lanreotide cause GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia (and glucose changes). Biliary pain plus a slow pulse in a controlled patient is the drug, not the disease.
takeaway: Somatostatin analogs: gallstones, GI upset, bradycardia.
discriminator: Octreotide → gallbladder and pulse; pegvisomant → liver tests.
